label: Riemannian Manifolds: The Toolkit
notes: This appendix collects the Riemannian-geometry machinery the book leans on for intrinsic statistics on shape spaces. Across printed pages 214 to 217 we review the metric, geodesics, the exponential map, curvature, and submersions, treating each not as abstract geometry but as the operational stage on which Frechet and Karcher means are actually computed.

label: The Riemannian Metric
notes: The Riemannian metric assigns a smoothly varying inner product to each tangent space, letting us measure lengths and angles of tangent vectors. Everything downstream depends on it: without a metric there is no notion of distance, no geodesic, and no intrinsic mean on a curved sample space such as a shape space.

label: Length and Energy of Curves
notes: Integrating the norm of a velocity vector gives a curve its length, and integrating the squared norm gives its energy. The metric makes both well defined. Minimizing length over curves joining two points produces the geodesic distance, the quantity that the book's intrinsic means are built to minimize on average over the data.

label: Levi-Civita Connection
notes: The Levi-Civita connection is the unique covariant derivative that is compatible with the metric and torsion-free. It tells us how to differentiate vector fields along curves and how to parallel transport tangent vectors, supplying the acceleration term whose vanishing defines a geodesic on the manifold.

label: Geodesics and Geodesic Distance
notes: Geodesics are curves of zero covariant acceleration; locally they minimize length and realize the geodesic distance between nearby points. This distance is the intrinsic ruler the book uses to define Frechet functions, so the entire theory of intrinsic location estimation rests on the geodesic structure described here.

label: Exponential and Logarithm Maps
notes: The exponential map sends a tangent vector at a point to the geodesic endpoint reached at unit time, linearizing the manifold near that point. Its local inverse, the logarithm map, lifts data back into the tangent space, where Euclidean computations such as averaging residuals become legitimate again.

label: Injectivity Radius and Normal Coordinates
notes: Within the injectivity radius the exponential map is a diffeomorphism, giving normal coordinates centered at a point where geodesics through the center are coordinate lines. Staying inside this radius is what guarantees that the logarithm map is single valued and that tangent-space statistics are unambiguous.

label: Sectional Curvature
notes: Sectional curvature measures how geodesics emanating from a point spread apart or reconverge along a two-plane in the tangent space. Positive curvature focuses geodesics, negative curvature spreads them, and this sign controls comparison theorems that bound how the squared-distance function behaves on the manifold.

label: Curvature and the Karcher Mean
notes: In a regular geodesic ball, curvature bounds make the squared-distance function geodesically convex, so the Frechet or Karcher mean is unique. Outside such a ball, on positively curved spaces, multiple minimizers can appear, which is exactly why the book imposes support conditions for its uniqueness theorems.

label: Riemannian Submersions and Shape Quotients
notes: A Riemannian submersion splits tangent vectors into vertical and horizontal parts and makes horizontal geodesics descend to geodesics below. Kendall shape spaces arise as such quotients of preshape spheres, so submersion geometry is how distances and means transfer from the sphere down to shape space.

label: Synthesis: Geometry to Inference
notes: Each tool maps to an inference step: the metric defines distance, geodesics define the Frechet function, exp and log move data to and from tangent space, curvature certifies uniqueness inside a regular ball, and submersions build shape space. Together they make nonparametric manifold inference rigorous rather than heuristic.
